title: Jupiter: King of the Planets
summary: Why Jupiter is called the king of the planets: its giant size, gas body and stripes, the Great Red Spot storm, its fast spin and long year, its large moons, and the spacecraft that study it.
poll: Jupiter is a more interesting planet to study than Earth.

versions.title: Jupiter, the Big One
versions.text:
Look up at night. Do you see a bright dot? It does not twinkle. It may be Jupiter!

Jupiter is a planet. It is the fifth one from the Sun. It is the biggest of them all. A thousand Earths could fit in it. It is a giant!

You can not stand on it. It has no hard ground. It is made of gas. Bands of clouds wrap it. They look like stripes.

It has a big red spot. The spot is a storm. It is wide. It is wider than Earth. It has spun for a long, long time.

Jupiter spins fast. A day there is just ten hours. But a year is long. It takes twelve of our years to go round the Sun.

Jupiter has lots of moons. Four are big. A man saw them long ago. He used a telescope. One moon has ice on top. There may be a sea down below.

Ships from Earth fly there. They help us learn.

versions.title: Jupiter: King of the Planets
versions.text:
On a clear night, look for a bright dot. It shines with a steady light and does not twinkle. It may be Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system.

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun. It is so big that more than one thousand Earths could fit inside it. That is why people call it a giant. Some even call it the king of the planets.

You could never stand on Jupiter, because it has no hard ground. It is made mostly of gas. Thick clouds wrap around it in colorful bands that look like stripes.

Jupiter has a huge red spot. The spot is really a giant storm. It is wider than the whole Earth. People have watched this storm swirl for more than one hundred years.

Jupiter spins faster than any other planet. A day there lasts only about ten hours. But Jupiter is far from the Sun, so it takes about twelve Earth years to travel around it once.

Jupiter has many moons. Four of them are large. A scientist named Galileo first saw them through a telescope more than four hundred years ago. One of these moons is covered in ice. Scientists think a salty sea may lie under it.

Today, spacecraft from Earth travel to Jupiter to study it up close.

versions.title: Jupiter: King of the Planets
versions.text:
On a clear night, look for a bright point of light. It shines steadily and does not twinkle. It may be Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system.

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun. It is so huge that more than one thousand Earths could fit inside it. Because of its size, people sometimes call it the king of the planets.

Unlike Earth, Jupiter has no solid surface to stand on. It is a ball made mostly of two gases, hydrogen and helium. Its thick atmosphere is full of clouds. They form colorful bands, so the planet looks striped.

Jupiter's most famous mark is the Great Red Spot. This spot is really a giant storm that is wider than our whole planet. People have watched it swirl for more than one hundred years, although it has slowly been shrinking.

Jupiter rotates faster than any other planet. One day there lasts just ten hours or so. However, because Jupiter is so far from the Sun, one trip around the Sun takes about twelve Earth years.

Jupiter has dozens of moons. Four of them are large. The scientist Galileo first spotted them through a telescope more than four hundred years ago. One, called Europa, is covered in ice, and scientists believe a salty ocean lies beneath it. Another, called Ganymede, is the largest moon in the solar system.

Today, spacecraft travel to Jupiter so that scientists can study this giant world up close.

versions.title: Jupiter: King of the Planets
versions.text:
On a clear night, look for a brilliant point of light that shines steadily rather than twinkling, because it may well be Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system. After the Moon and Venus, it is frequently one of the brightest objects visible in the night sky.

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun, and it is so enormous that more than one thousand Earths could fit inside it. Its mass is more than twice that of all the other planets combined, which is why people sometimes describe it as the king of the planets.

Unlike Earth, Jupiter has no solid surface on which a visitor could stand. It is a gas giant composed predominantly of hydrogen and helium, the same two elements that make up most of the Sun. Its thick atmosphere is filled with clouds that stretch into colorful parallel bands, giving the planet its distinctive striped appearance.

One of Jupiter's most celebrated features is the Great Red Spot, a gigantic storm that is wider than our entire planet. Astronomers have observed it swirling for more than one hundred and fifty years, although measurements show that it has gradually been shrinking.

Jupiter rotates faster than any other planet, so a single day there lasts only about ten hours. However, because Jupiter travels at such a great distance from the Sun, one complete orbit requires approximately twelve Earth years. The planet also generates an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field, the strongest of any planet, which produces dazzling auroras near its poles.

Jupiter possesses dozens of moons, and four of them are especially large. Galileo first observed these four through a telescope more than four hundred years ago, and his discovery helped demonstrate that not everything in the sky circles Earth. Europa is covered in ice, and scientists believe a salty ocean lies beneath its frozen crust. Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, while Io is the most volcanic world currently known.

Today, robotic spacecraft such as Juno, which began orbiting Jupiter in 2016, allow scientists to investigate this giant world and its fascinating moons in remarkable detail.

versions.title: Jupiter: King of the Planets
versions.text:
On a clear night, an attentive observer may notice a brilliant point of light that shines steadily rather than twinkling, and that luminous point may well be Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system. After the Moon and Venus, it is frequently one of the most conspicuous objects in the nocturnal sky, visible even to observers who possess no specialized astronomical equipment.

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun, and its dimensions are so extraordinary that more than one thousand Earths could theoretically fit inside it. Its mass exceeds twice the combined mass of all the other planets, which explains why commentators occasionally characterize it as the king of the planets.

Unlike Earth, Jupiter possesses no solid surface on which a visitor could stand, because it is a gas giant composed predominantly of hydrogen and helium, the identical elements that constitute most of the Sun. Its dense atmosphere contains turbulent clouds that stretch into colorful parallel bands, generating the planet's distinctive striped appearance.

Among Jupiter's most celebrated characteristics is the Great Red Spot, a gigantic atmospheric storm considerably wider than our entire planet. Astronomers have continuously monitored it for more than one hundred and fifty years, although careful measurements indicate that it has gradually been diminishing in size.

Jupiter rotates more rapidly than any other planet, so a single day there lasts only about ten hours. Nevertheless, because Jupiter travels at such an immense distance from the Sun, one complete orbit requires approximately twelve Earth years. The planet additionally generates an exceptionally powerful magnetic field, the strongest belonging to any planet, which produces spectacular auroras surrounding its poles.

Jupiter possesses dozens of moons, and four of them are exceptionally large. Galileo first observed these four satellites through a telescope more than four hundred years ago, and his discovery provided important evidence that not every celestial object revolves around Earth. Europa is encased in ice, and scientists hypothesize that a salty ocean lies concealed beneath its frozen crust. Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, whereas Io is the most volcanically active world currently identified.

Contemporary robotic spacecraft, including Juno, which began orbiting Jupiter in 2016, enable scientists to investigate this colossal world and its fascinating satellites in remarkable detail, and additional missions are presently traveling toward Europa to examine its mysterious hidden ocean more thoroughly.

MID.modelAnswer: One feature of Jupiter that is different from Earth is that it has no solid surface at all, since it is really a giant ball made mostly of gas with a thick, swirling atmosphere instead of ground to stand on. Scientists first studied Jupiter's four largest moons through a telescope centuries ago, and they now believe one of them, Europa, hides a salty ocean beneath its icy surface.

HIGH.prompt: The article calls Jupiter the king of the planets. Do you agree that this name fits? Support your opinion with at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion about the name.
I supported it with at least three facts from the article.
I used precise vocabulary, including at least two key words.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that "king of the planets" fits Jupiter perfectly. Its sheer mass is greater than all the other planets in the solar system combined, and it is built almost entirely from hydrogen and helium gas rather than solid rock. Jupiter also commands a vast system of moons, including one with volcanic eruptions and a powerful magnetic field that shields the whole system around it. Robotic spacecraft still travel there today just to study this giant world and its many moons up close, which shows how much influence and mystery Jupiter still holds over our solar system.
